Introduction to Individual Decision-Maki: While reading this lecture, build a small preference table before writing any utility numbers. Mark which comparisons are rankings, which comparisons involve uncertainty, and which claims would change if the utility scale were stretched. The work is to separate choice order from psychological interpretation.
Representation of Games: For each example, redraw the situation twice: once as a compact action table and once as a timeline. Then write what each representation hides. The work is to notice that representation is already an argument about timing, information, and available choices.
Dominance: Make a column-by-column deletion log. For every proposed dominated action, record the rival contingency, the two payoffs being compared, and whether the inequality survives. The work is to earn the deletion by proof instead of by taste or plausibility.
Rationalizability: Pick one action that looks odd and try to rescue it with a belief about the other player. If no belief makes it optimal, identify the payoff comparison that blocks it. The work is to distinguish individual defensibility from final prediction.
Nash Equilibrium: Take every proposed outcome and run a one-player deviation audit. Freeze everyone else, test one player, then move to the next player. The work is to stop asking whether the outcome feels good and ask whether unilateral regret remains.
Imperfect Competition: Write each firm's profit as depending on its own choice and the rival's choice before solving anything. Then derive a best response against a named rival action. The work is to see market power as relational rather than as isolated monopoly logic.
Zero-Sum Games: Add the players' payoffs in each cell before using zero-sum language. If the total is fixed, compute what each action protects against; if not, name the shared gains or losses. The work is to keep security reasoning inside its proper boundary.
Backward Induction: Start from the last decision nodes and write the action the future player will actually want there. Replace those nodes with values before moving earlier. The work is to make present threats answer to future incentives instead of narrative force.
Negotiation: Separate total surplus, each side's outside option, and the cost of waiting. Then change one of those three inputs and trace how the bargaining position changes. The work is to translate toughness into continuation values rather than personality.
Subgame-Perfect Nash Equilibrium: For every threat or promise, jump to the history where it would be carried out and solve from there. The work is to test credibility locally, not just at the initial node where the threat changes behavior.
One-Shot Deviation Principle and Bargain: Choose a history and change exactly one current action while keeping the continuation plan fixed. Record the immediate gain and future loss. The work is to understand why a local deviation test is powerful only under the theorem's conditions.
Finitely Repeated Games: Solve the final period first and write what future punishment is unavailable there. Then move one period earlier and repeat. The work is to see how a known endpoint can travel backward through incentives. If cooperation survives in your notes, name the extra force stopping the unraveling.
Infinitely Repeated Games: Write the cooperate path and the cheat-then-punish path side by side with discount factors attached. The work is to compare today's temptation with the present value of future consequences, not simply to say repetition creates trust.
Folk Theorem: Pick one candidate long-run payoff and check three gates: feasibility, individual rationality, and punishment credibility. The work is to treat the theorem as a supportability test, then separately ask what selects one supported outcome.
Implicit Cartels: Name the cheating gain, the monitoring signal, and the punishment that rivals are supposed to impose. Then ask whether punishment is itself profitable. The work is to separate a repeated-game mechanism from legal evidence of explicit agreement. Also mark whether demand shocks could be mistaken for cheating, because monitoring quality is part of the incentive story.
Bayesian Games: Before solving, list the hidden types, who observes each type, and the prior probabilities. Then write a strategy as a rule for every type. The work is to stop using uncertainty as a vague excuse and put it into the model.
Bayesian Nash Equilibrium: Applications: Check incentives type by type. Hold the other players' type-contingent rules fixed and ask whether each type wants to deviate. The work is to avoid hiding a failed low-type or high-type incentive inside an average-player calculation. If one type fails, the whole strategy rule fails even when the average payoff looks fine.
Auctions: Split each bid into chance of winning, payment if winning, and value if winning. Then change the auction format and repeat the split. The work is to see a bid as a strategic response to rules, not as a transparent value label.
Revenue Equivalence: Before applying the theorem, write the assumptions as a checklist: allocation rule, lowest-type payoff, symmetry, independence, risk neutrality, and entry conditions. The work is to learn what makes equivalence fragile, not just what makes it elegant.
Ad Auctions: Separate bid, quality score, click probability, slot allocation, and payment. Then ask which piece changes under the platform rule being discussed. The work is to keep user attention, advertiser incentives, and platform revenue from collapsing into one score.
Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium: Write strategies and beliefs in pairs. After every observed action, ask whether Bayes rule pins down the belief and whether the action is optimal under that belief. The work is to keep off-path assumptions visible.
Signaling: For each type, compare the payoff from sending the signal with the payoff from imitating another type's signal. Then update the receiver's belief from the behavior that survives. The work is to see information as an incentive pattern. If both types choose the same signal, label the result pooling before claiming anything was revealed.
Bargaining with Incomplete Information: After any offer or price, recompute who accepts. Do not reuse the original population average. The work is to see bargaining as selection plus surplus division, where the act of accepting can reveal hidden type.
Cheap Talk: Write what each sender type wants the receiver to do, then ask what message each type would send. The work is to decide whether words separate types, pool types, or become uninformative because incentives point every type to the same message.
Common Knowledge: For every fact in the example, label whether it is private, mutual, public, or common knowledge. Then name the coordinated action that needs higher-order confidence. The work is to distinguish shared information from shared awareness.
